newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan killer says rigid education behind beheading.
newsitem.headline: Japan killer says rigid education behind beheading.

text.p: A person who claims to have killed and beheaded a schoolboy in Kobe has said in a letter to the western Japanese city's newspaper that he murdered to take revenge on a rigid education system.
"It is a big mistake to think that I am a childish killer who can only kill children," said a letter received by the Kobe Shimbun daily on Wednesday.

The letter, printed in major Japanese newspapers on Friday, repeated warnings of future killings and taunts against police that were in a note attached to the severed head of 11-year-old Jun Hase, whose mutilated corpse was found on May 27.
Police said the letter did not appear to be a hoax because it contained some of the phrases in the previous note that investigators had not made public and that only the killer would know.

The sentence "I've really, really wanted to see a person die," included in a note appended to the 1,400 word letter, was found with the head but had not been made public, news reports quoted police as saying.
The writer, describing himself as an "invisible man" with "no nationality", urged police to take him seriously because he was risking his life committing crimes he could be hanged for.
"I'm not going so far as to say police should risk their lives, but pursue me with more anger and determination," he said.
The writer suggested that the murder of the boy, whose head was placed at the iron gates of a junior high school, was an act of revenge against the "compulsory education which created me".
The writer also expressed anger at police statements and media reports which had mistaken his name.
The author said the name Seito Sakakibara found on the note attached to the boy's head was "not a code, a puzzle or a nickname or fabrication, but my real name."
"If even once again my name is misread or something happens to make me unhappy, I'll destroy three vegetables each week," the letter said.
The cryptic note found with the body spoke of killing "dirty vegetables" in what police said was a reference to people or children.

Police have mobilised 500 detectives to solve the crime, which occurred near a school where two young schoolgirls were attacked -- one fatally -- by a knife-wielding man in March and several animals were killed and mutilated.
Police said there was no evidence so far that the cases were linked.

The killing has sent shockwaves across Japan and has caused new anguish for the residents of Kobe, many of whom have only recently rebuilt homes and lives shattered by the powerful earthquake which killed 6,000 people in January 1995.
